claim: Postmenopausal atherosclerosis has been attributed to estrogen deficiency.
source: Postmenopausal atherosclerosis (AS) has been attributed to estrogen deficiency.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established scientific understanding.

claim: The beneficial effect of hormone replacement therapy is lost in late postmenopausal women with atherogenesis.
source: However, the beneficial effect of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is lost in late postmenopausal women with atherogenesis.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to clinical studies mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: A negative correlation has been observed between aging-related systemic iron deposition and ERα expression in postmenopausal AS patients.
source: A negative correlation has been observed between aging-related systemic iron deposition and ERα expression in postmenopausal AS patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1 showing ferritin, iron content, and ERα expression in patient samples.

claim: Estradiol treatment had contrasting effects on ERα expression in early versus late postmenopausal mice in an ovariectomized Apoe-/- mouse model.
source: In an ovariectomized Apoe-/- mouse model, estradiol treatment had contrasting effects on ERα expression in early versus late postmenopausal mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ERα expression was inhibited by iron treatment in cell culture and iron-overloaded mice.
source: ERα expression was inhibited by iron treatment in cell culture and iron-overloaded mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3, 4, and 5 showing ERα downregulation with iron treatment.

claim: Combined treatment with estradiol and iron further decreased ERα expression.
source: Combined treatment with estradiol and iron further decreased ERα expression, and the latter effect was mediated by iron-regulated E3 ligase Mdm2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5 showing synergistic effects of E2 and iron on ERα.

claim: The decrease in ERα expression by combined estradiol and iron treatment was mediated by iron-regulated E3 ligase Mdm2.
source: Combined treatment with estradiol and iron further decreased ERα expression, and the latter effect was mediated by iron-regulated E3 ligase Mdm2.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing Mdm2 upregulation and its role in ERα degradation.

claim: Cellular cholesterol efflux was reduced in response to iron and estradiol treatment.
source: In line with these observations, cellular cholesterol efflux was reduced, and endothelial homeostasis was disrupted.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced ABCA1 expression and increased lipid accumulation in Figure 4G.

claim: Endothelial homeostasis was disrupted by iron and estradiol treatment.
source: In line with these observations, cellular cholesterol efflux was reduced, and endothelial homeostasis was disrupted.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced eNOS and VEGF expression and impaired angiogenesis in Figures 4H, 4I.

claim: Atherosclerosis was aggravated by combined iron and estradiol treatment.
source: Consequently, AS was aggravated.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2 and 3 showing increased plaque area with E2 treatment in late postmenopausal mice.

claim: Systemic iron chelation attenuated estradiol-triggered progressive AS in late postmenopausal mice.
source: Accordingly, systemic iron chelation attenuated estradiol-triggered progressive AS in late postmenopausal mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing reduced plaque area with DFP treatment.

claim: Iron and estradiol together downregulate ERα through Mdm2-mediated proteolysis.
source: Thus, iron and estradiol together downregulate ERα through Mdm2-mediated proteolysis, providing a potential explanation for failures of HRT in late postmenopausal subjects with aging-related iron accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing Mdm2 upregulation, ERα ubiquitination, and proteasomal degradation.

claim: Immediate HRT after menopause, along with appropriate iron chelation, might provide benefits from atherosclerosis.
source: This study suggests that immediate HRT after menopause, along with appropriate iron chelation, might provide benefits from AS.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Atherosclerosis is the leading cause of cardiovascular disease-associated deaths worldwide.
source: Atherosclerosis (AS) is the leading cause of cardiovascular disease-associated deaths worldwide (Moss et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Moss et al., 2019.

claim: Postmenopausal women confront an increasing risk of AS owing to estrogen deficiency and disturbance of the estrogen receptor regulatory network.
source: It has been well recognized that postmenopausal women confront an increasing risk of AS owing to estrogen deficiency and disturbance of the estrogen receptor (ER) regulatory network (Moss et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Moss et al., 2019.

claim: The Women's Health Initiative and the Heart and Estrogen/Progestin Replacement Study reported that the atheroprotective effect of HRT in late postmenopausal women is lost or even worsened.
source: The Women's Health Initiative and the Heart and Estrogen/Progestin Replacement Study reported that the atheroprotective effect of HRT in late postmenopausal women (commonly ages over 65) is lost or even worsened (Hlatky et al., 2002; Rocca et al., 2014; Rossouw et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The atheroprotective effect of estrogen is attributed to its interaction with estrogen receptor α (ERα).
source: In general, the atheroprotective effect of estrogen is attributed to its interaction with estrogen receptor α (ERα), which participates in foam cell formation and vascular remodeling (Murphy, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Murphy, 2011.

claim: ERα deletion is reported to induce adiposity and increase atherosclerotic lesion size.
source: ERα deletion is reported to induce adiposity and increase atherosclerotic lesion size since the promoters of lipid metabolism-related genes, such as Tgm2, Apoe, and Abca1, contain ERα-binding sites (Ribas et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ribas et al., 2011.

claim: The promoters of lipid metabolism-related genes, such as Tgm2, Apoe, and Abca1, contain ERα-binding sites.
source: ERα deletion is reported to induce adiposity and increase atherosclerotic lesion size since the promoters of lipid metabolism-related genes, such as Tgm2, Apoe, and Abca1, contain ERα-binding sites (Ribas et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ribas et al., 2011.

claim: Estrogen binds to ERα tethered to the plasma membrane, which can stimulate vasodilatation via an endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS)-dependent pathway.
source: In addition, estrogen binds to ERα tethered to the plasma membrane, which can stimulate vasodilatation via an endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS)-dependent pathway (Gavin et al., 2009; Teoh et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gavin et al., 2009 and Teoh et al., 2020.

claim: VEGF promotes angiogenesis and is transcriptionally regulated by the E2-ERα complex.
source: Moreover, VEGF promotes angiogenesis and is transcriptionally regulated by the E2-ERα complex (Gu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gu et al., 2018.

claim: ERα expression decreases after menopause.
source: ERα expression decreases after menopause (Gavin et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2019), suggesting the critical role of ERα in blood vessel function in healthy pre- and postmenopausal women.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gavin et al., 2009 and Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Estrogen functions as an ERα activator upon binding.
source: Upon binding, estrogen functions as an ERα activator (Lung et al., 2020) and initiates ERα dimerization and translocation into the nucleus.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lung et al., 2020.

claim: Estrogen treatment in vitro leads to a marked increase in Esr1 mRNA through the binding of the E2-ERα complex to estrogen-responsive elements in the promoter region of Esr1.
source: Estrogen treatment in vitro leads to a marked increase in Esr1 (gene that encodes ERα) mRNA through the binding of the E2-ERα complex to estrogen-responsive elements (EREs) in the promoter region of Esr1 (Pinzone et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pinzone et al., 2004.

claim: Estrogen binding to ERα rapidly stimulates ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of ERα.
source: Estrogen binding to ERα also rapidly stimulates ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of ERα (Pinzone et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pinzone et al., 2004.

claim: Ubiquitin ligases that have been implicated in ERα regulation include BRCA1, MDM2, SCFSKP2, and E6AP.
source: Ubiquitin ligases that have been implicated in ERα regulation include BRCA1, MDM2, SKP1–CUL1–F-box S-phase kinase-associated protein 2 (SCFSKP2), and E6-associated protein (E6AP), all of which promote estrogen-induced transcriptional activity with cell-type selectivity (Zhou and Slingerland, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhou and Slingerland, 2014.

claim: MDM2 is a single-subunit RING finger E3 protein.
source: Of these, MDM2 is a single-subunit RING finger E3 protein, which does not always inversely correlate with ERα levels in cancer cells (Duong et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Duong et al., 2007.

claim: Estrogen regulates systemic iron homeostasis through hepcidin.
source: Estrogen also regulates systemic iron homeostasis through hepcidin, an antimicrobial peptide of 25 amino acids that mediates endocytosis and degradation of the ferrous iron exporter ferroportin 1 (Fpn1) (Nemeth et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nemeth et al., 2004.

claim: Hepcidin is an antimicrobial peptide of 25 amino acids that mediates endocytosis and degradation of ferroportin 1.
source: Estrogen also regulates systemic iron homeostasis through hepcidin, an antimicrobial peptide of 25 amino acids that mediates endocytosis and degradation of the ferrous iron exporter ferroportin 1 (Fpn1) (Nemeth et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nemeth et al., 2004.

claim: The dimeric E2-ERα complex binds to an ERE site within the promoter of the hepcidin gene to inhibit its expression.
source: The dimeric E2-ERα complex binds to an ERE site within the promoter of the hepcidin gene (Hamp) to inhibit its expression (Hou et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hou et al., 2012.

claim: E2 elevates circulating iron to compensate for blood loss during menstruation.
source: Hence, E2 elevates circulating iron to compensate for blood loss during menstruation (Badenhorst et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Badenhorst et al., 2021.

claim: E2 declines by >90% after menopause.
source: However, E2 declines by >90% after menopause, while systemic iron content increases slowly by steady iron uptake over the years.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about hormonal changes after menopause.

claim: Systemic iron content increases slowly by steady iron uptake over the years after menopause.
source: However, E2 declines by >90% after menopause, while systemic iron content increases slowly by steady iron uptake over the years.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about iron accumulation after menopause.

claim: Serum ferritin in postmenopausal women increased by 2–3 times compared with premenopausal women.
source: Serum ferritin in postmenopausal women increased by 2–3 times compared with premenopausal women (Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2013.

claim: Iron overload is a risk factor for atherosclerosis.
source: We and others have previously reported that iron overload is a risk factor for atherosclerosis (Cai et al., 2020; Vinchi et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cai et al., 2020 and Vinchi et al., 2020.

claim: Ferritin and iron levels were significantly increased in plaques and serum in the late postmenopausal group compared to the early postmenopausal group.
source: The results showed that ferritin and iron levels were significantly increased in plaques and serum in the LPM compared to that in the EPM (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: Serum hepcidin levels increased in the late postmenopausal group.
source: Consistently, serum hepcidin levels increased in the LPM group (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Plaque ERα expression was lower in the late postmenopausal group than in the early postmenopausal group.
source: By contrast, plaque ERα expression was lower in the LPM than in the EPM (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Serum cholesterol and triglycerides were elevated in the late postmenopausal group.
source: In addition, serum cholesterol and triglycerides were elevated in the LPM (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: E2 administration in the early postmenopausal stage significantly reduced plaque formation and mouse weight.
source: Although E2 administration in the EPM significantly reduced plaque formation and mouse weight, it remarkably promoted atherosclerotic development and weight gain in late application (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), exactly as observed in humans (Hlatky et al., 2002; Rossouw et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: E2 administration in the late postmenopausal stage remarkably promoted atherosclerotic development and weight gain.
source: Although E2 administration in the EPM significantly reduced plaque formation and mouse weight, it remarkably promoted atherosclerotic development and weight gain in late application (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), exactly as observed in humans (Hlatky et al., 2002; Rossouw et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and is consistent with human studies.

claim: ERα protein levels were markedly lower in late postmenopausal mice than in early postmenopausal mice.
source: The results showed markedly lower ERα protein levels in the LPM mice than in the EPM mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ERα expression was further reduced in late postmenopausal mice after E2 treatment but remained constantly high in early postmenopausal mice.
source: More strikingly, ERα expression was further reduced in LPM mice after E2 treatment but remained constantly high in EPM mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ABCA1, VEGF, and eNOS were all positively correlated with ERα expression.
source: Hence, we assessed three ERα downstream proteins, ABCA1, a lipid exporter whose gene promoter is predicted to have ERE, VEGF, an activator of angiogenesis, and eNOS, a modulator of vasoconstriction and vascular repair. They were all positively correlated with ERα expression (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ABCA1 expression in peritoneal macrophages responded to E2 treatment similarly as observed in aortic tissue.
source: We, therefore, isolated peritoneal macrophages from early and late OVX mice after E2 treatment and found that ABCA1 expression responded to E2 treatment similarly as observed in aortic tissue, with no change in ERα and VEGF, but keeping at high levels (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Serum cholesterol and triglycerides negatively correlated with ABCA1.
source: In line with this observation, serum cholesterol and triglycerides negatively correlated with ABCA1 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Ferritin was reduced in peritoneal macrophages in the early postmenopausal group in response to E2 treatment.
source: In the isolated macrophages, ferritin was reduced in the EPM group, while Fpn1 was elevated in both stages in response to E2 treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Fpn1 was elevated in peritoneal macrophages in both early and late postmenopausal stages in response to E2 treatment.
source: In the isolated macrophages, ferritin was reduced in the EPM group, while Fpn1 was elevated in both stages in response to E2 treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Iron levels in tissues (aorta and liver) were significantly higher in late postmenopausal mice compared to early postmenopausal mice.
source: Iron levels in tissues, aorta and liver, were significantly higher in the LPM mice (Figure 2G, LPM vs. EPM without E2 treatment).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: E2 treatment elevated serum iron while lowering tissue iron in both early and late postmenopausal stages.
source: Interestingly, E2 treatment elevated serum iron while lowering tissue iron in both EPM and LPM stages (Figure 2G, H and E treatment vs. saline), suggesting impaired iron homeostasis in the plaque area, particularly in macrophages (Figure 2E) and confirming that estrogen modulates iron homeostasis as previously suggested (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2E, 2G, and 2H, and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Atherosclerosis was significantly enhanced in E2-treated Apoe-/- Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 mice at both early and late postmenopausal stages compared to saline groups.
source: Figure 3B and C show the severity of AS, which was significantly enhanced in the E2-treated groups at both ages compared to the saline groups of Apoe-/- Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Macrophage Fpn1 knockout mice displayed a larger lesion area after E2 treatment at the early and late postmenopausal stages.
source: Notably, macrophage Fpn1 KO mice displayed a larger lesion area after E2 treatment at the EPM and LPM stages (Figure 3C), suggesting a dominant influence of iron on the effects of the E2 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Specific iron overload in macrophages was sufficient to cause a significant increase in the lesion area in the late postmenopausal group.
source: In particular, the specific iron overload in macrophages, characteristic of the mouse model used, was sufficient to cause a significant increase in the lesion area in the LPM group (Figure 3C, lower panel), reproducing previous observations (Cai et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and is consistent with previous observations.

claim: Iron levels in tissues (aorta/liver) were higher in Apoe-/- Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 compared to Apoe-/- mice.
source: Iron levels in tissues (aorta/liver) were higher in Apoe-/- Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 compared to Apoe-/- mice, as revealed by ferrozine assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B for EPM groups and Figure 3D for LPM groups) and further supported by higher ferritin content (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B for EPM and Figure 3E for LPM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, 3E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Serum iron was lower in Apoe-/-Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 mice at the early and late postmenopausal stages.
source: On the contrary, serum iron was lower in Apoe-/-Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 mice at the EPM and LPM stages (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: E2 administration did not significantly lower the iron and ferritin levels in the aorta and liver of Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 mice.
source: However, E2 administration did not significantly lower the iron and ferritin levels in the aorta and liver (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), confirming that Fpn1 acts as an iron exporter and that macrophages play a crucial role in response to E2 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, 3E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: E2 administration significantly increased serum iron levels in the late postmenopausal group of Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 mice.
source: E2 administration significantly increased serum iron levels in the LPM group (Figure 3F) and mildly increased serum iron levels in the EPM group (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that other factors may contribute to the aging-related response to estrogen.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ERα was downregulated in the aorta of Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 mice and further downregulated by E2 treatment.
source: Of note, ERα was downregulated in the aorta of the Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 mice and further downregulated by E2 treatment, accompanied by reduced expression of ABCA1 and VEGF (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that both iron alone and iron plus E2 could downregulate ERα expression in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Serum cholesterol and triglycerides were increased in the Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 mice and further increased by E2 treatment.
source: Consistent with the severity of atherosclerosis and the alteration of ERα and its target gene ABCA1, serum cholesterol and triglycerides were increased in the Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 mice and further increased by E2 treatment (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Downregulation of ERα expression triggered by FAC with or without E2 was observed in time- and concentration-dependent manners.
source: Downregulation of ERα expression triggered by FAC with or without E2 was observed in time- and concentration-dependent manners (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: ERα downregulation by iron was confirmed in J774a.1 cells, primary peritoneal macrophages, and HUVECs and could be partially suppressed by iron chelation.
source: Such downregulation was confirmed in all tested cell types and could be partially suppressed by iron chelation (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: Significantly more lipid accumulation was observed in J774a.1 cells in the E2-treated plus iron overload group than in the other groups.
source: To examine the capacity of lipid export when ERα was downregulated, we loaded J774a.1 with oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL) and observed significantly more lipid accumulation in the E2-treated plus iron overload group than in the other groups (Figure 4G), suggesting a tendency of macrophages to be converted into foam cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: E2 together with iron inhibited angiogenesis in HUVECs.
source: Angiogenesis assays were also performed and showed that E2, together with iron, inhibited angiogenesis (Figure 4H), which has been demonstrated to increase the risk of macrophage adhesion and intraplaque hemorrhage (Chang and Nguyen, 2021; Mao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Reduced levels of eNOS were revealed by ELISA in HUVECs treated with E2 and iron.
source: The reduced levels of eNOS were also revealed by ELISA in HUVECs treated with E2 and iron (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Both macrophages and endothelial cells are the effectors of E2 in iron-mediated worsening by downregulation of ERα in the development of atherosclerosis.
source: Overall, our data strongly support that both macrophages and endothelial cells are the effectors of E2 in iron-mediated worsening by downregulation of ERα in the development of AS.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: ERα protein levels were significantly elevated in the presence of E2 and excess iron when treated with MG132, a proteasome inhibitor.
source: To test this possibility, we treated J774a.1 cells with MG132, a proteasome inhibitor, and observed that ERα protein levels were significantly elevated in the presence of E2 and excess iron (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The half-life of ERα was shortened in the E2 + FAC group.
source: Treatment with cycloheximide (CHX), an inhibitor of eukaryotic translation, showed that the half-life of ERα was shortened in the E2 + FAC group (Figure 5B), suggesting a faster turnover rate of ERα in the presence of E2 plus excess iron, verifying the activation of ERα proteasome degradation pathway (Zhou and Slingerland, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Much more ubiquitinated and degraded ERα was observed in the presence of E2 and excess iron than in other conditions.
source: We then detected the ubiquitination levels of ERα by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting. The results showed much more ubiquitinated and degraded ERα in the presence of E2 and excess iron than in other conditions (Figure 5C), further supporting the proteolysis-dependent pathway for ERα degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mdm2 was upregulated in the FAC and E2 + FAC groups in J774a.1 cells.
source: However, Mdm2 was upregulated in the FAC and E2 + FAC groups (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Treatment of J774a.1 cells and HUVECs with the Mdm2 inhibitor Nutlin-3 demonstrated iron-dependent Mdm2-mediated degradation of ERα.
source: Treatment of the J774a.1 cells and HUVECs with the Mdm2 inhibitor Nutlin-3 demonstrated iron-dependent Mdm2-mediated degradation of ERα (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: Mdm2 expression was upregulated at the late postmenopausal stage compared with the early postmenopausal stage both in female mice's aorta and in AS patients' plaques.
source: Importantly and consistently, Mdm2 expression was upregulated at the LPM stage compared with the EPM stage both in female mice's aorta and in AS patients' plaques (Figure 5G and H), which is precisely opposite to ERα expression (Figure 1B), and this effect was significantly enhanced at the LPM stage mice when E2 was administrated (Figures 2D and E and 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and 5H.

claim: Mdm2 is responsible for E2-triggered ERα deficiency under iron overload conditions or in late postmenopausal women.
source: Our results indicate that Mdm2 is responsible for E2-triggered ERα deficiency under iron overload conditions or in LPM women.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Iron chelation attenuated the plaque-accelerated development of atherosclerosis in late postmenopausal mice.
source: Indeed, iron chelation attenuated the plaque-accelerated development of AS (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: The contents of serum cholesterol and triglycerides were significantly diminished by iron chelation compared with the E2-only group.
source: The contents of serum cholesterol and triglycerides compared with those in the E2-only group were significantly diminished (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Iron chelation significantly upregulated aortic ERα expression, along with the upregulation of ABCA1 and VEGF.
source: We then detected aortic ERα expression and found significant upregulation by iron restriction, along with the upregulation of ABCA1 and VEGF (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Iron chelation by DFP significantly reduced Mdm2 expression.
source: In contrast, iron chelation by DFP significantly reduced Mdm2 expression (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Late postmenopausal HRT-induced ERα deficiency is, at least partially, iron overload-mediated.
source: In agreement with our previous findings in cell-based assays, these results corroborate the concept that late postmenopausal HRT-induced ERα deficiency is, at least partially, iron overload-mediated.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The non-atheroprotective effects of E2 in the late postmenopausal stage result from aging-mediated iron accumulation.
source: Thus, the non-atheroprotective effects of E2 in the LPM result from aging-mediated iron accumulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The developmental course of atherosclerosis was highly accelerated in Apoe-/-Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 mice compared with Apoe-/-.
source: We reported previously that the developmental course of AS was highly accelerated in Apoe-/-Fpn1Lyz2/Lyz2 mice compared with Apoe-/-(Cai et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cai et al., 2020.

claim: This study provides the first experimental evidence that iron overload facilitates ERα proteolysis, which is potentiated in the presence of E2 and reverses the anti-atherogenic effect of E2.
source: The present study provides the first experimental evidence that iron overload facilitates ERα proteolysis, which is potentiated in the presence of E2 and reverses the anti-atherogenic effect of E2 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.

claim: The combination of HRT and iron restriction therapy might be a long-term strategy for the preventive effects of E2 from the development of atherosclerosis in postmenopausal women.
source: We propose that the combination of HRT and iron restriction therapy might be a long-term strategy for the preventive effects of E2 from the development of AS in postmenopausal women.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: Iron accumulation occurs naturally and gradually after menopause.
source: Iron accumulation occurs naturally and gradually after menopause.
evidence: This statement is shown in Figure 7.

claim: In early postmenopause, iron retention was mild, and ERα was responsive to HRT application to achieve protective effects.
source: In early postmenopausal (EPM), iron retention was mild, and ERα was responsive to HRT application to achieve protective effects.
evidence: This statement is shown in Figure 7 and is supported by experimental data.

claim: When iron overload is significant in late postmenopause, Mdm2 is upregulated along with ERα downregulation.
source: However, when iron overload is significant in late postmenopausal (LPM), Mdm2 is upregulated along with ERα downregulation.
evidence: This statement is shown in Figure 7 and is supported by experimental data.

claim: The negative correlation between Mdm2 and ERα is potentiated by the application of HRT and iron accumulation with aging.
source: This negative correlation is potentiated by the application of HRT and iron accumulation with aging.
evidence: This statement is shown in Figure 7 and is supported by experimental data.

claim: HRT use avails to aggravate the progression of atherosclerosis in the late postmenopausal period.
source: Therefore, HRT use avails to aggravate the progression of AS in the LPM period.
evidence: This statement is shown in Figure 7 and is supported by experimental data.

claim: Iron chelation reverses the adverse effect of HRT and attenuates the accelerated development of atherosclerosis.
source: Iron chelation, however, reverses the adverse effect of HRT and attenuates the accelerated development of AS, suggesting a protective role of appropriate iron restriction in the LPM stage.
evidence: This statement is shown in Figure 7 and is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Appropriate iron restriction has a protective role in the late postmenopausal stage.
source: Iron chelation, however, reverses the adverse effect of HRT and attenuates the accelerated development of AS, suggesting a protective role of appropriate iron restriction in the LPM stage.
evidence: This statement is shown in Figure 7 and is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.
